threads.thread_goal: Align on incident scenarios, scope, and playbook structure.

messages.text: Good morning team. We're kicking off the Crisis Communication Playbook project today. The goal is to have a clear, multi-channel playbook ready before the next quarterly safety drill—that's 21 days from now. We need to cover incident escalation, media handling, internal briefings, and training. Let's start by mapping out which incident scenarios we should prioritize in v1. I'm thinking we focus on 4–6 core types that cover most of our on-site security risks. Who wants to lead the scenario mapping?

I can help with that. From my time in security, I've seen a few patterns—unauthorized access attempts, suspicious packages, medical emergencies on-site, and equipment failures that could look like incidents. Those are the main ones we deal with. I'll start documenting what we currently do for each.

Good start. From a PR angle, I'd add one more: external threats or public safety concerns that might trigger media interest. We need to be ready for that scenario too. Once we have the full list, we should validate it with ops and legal to make sure we're not missing anything critical.

Agreed. So that gives us five solid scenarios: unauthorized access, suspicious packages, medical emergencies, equipment failures, and external threats. I think that's a good foundation for v1. Let's also think about the playbook structure—who owns what section? I'm thinking we need clear ownership for escalation, media response, internal comms, and training.

I can take the media response section and the channel strategy. That ties into T4 and T7 for holding statements and multi-channel mapping. I'll need input from legal on what we can and can't say, but I can draft the templates.

I'll handle the training and internal briefing side. I can work on T5 and T6—the briefing templates and training content. I want to make sure the language is accessible for non-specialist staff, so I'll test it with a small group before we finalize.

Perfect. That leaves escalation scripts and quick-reference checklists for me and 47290. We'll own T3 and T8. I'll draft the escalation script, and we'll test it with security staff to make sure it's clear under pressure. The checklist needs to be simple enough to use in a real incident.

I'll help with testing the script. I know what works and what doesn't from the ground level. But I want to make sure we keep it really simple—no jargon that security staff won't understand in the moment.

One thing we should clarify: who's responsible for the overall playbook consolidation and version control? And do we have a sign-off process with legal and ops before we distribute? That's T12 and it's critical.

Good catch. I'll own the final consolidation and make sure we have legal and ops sign-off before distribution. We'll need to set up a review gate about a week before the drill. Let me also confirm the ownership matrix in writing so everyone knows who to go to for each section.
I'll document the RACI matrix and share it by EOD tomorrow. That way everyone has clarity on who decides what and who needs to be consulted.

Sounds good. So to recap: we've locked in five incident scenarios, assigned ownership for each major section, and we have a consolidation and sign-off plan. I think we're ready to move into detailed drafting. I'll start on the training materials this week.

threads.thread_goal: Define on-site escalation scripts and quick-reference checklists.

messages.text: I've drafted the on-site incident escalation script based on the five scenarios we agreed on. The script walks security staff through: (1) initial assessment, (2) immediate safety steps, (3) notification to control center, (4) escalation to management, and (5) handoff to PR/legal if needed. I've kept the language plain and the steps numbered so it's easy to follow under stress. See A2 for the draft. I'd like 47290 to review this from a practical standpoint—does it match what actually happens on the ground?

I'll review it. One thing I want to check: does it account for the radio communication delays we sometimes get? And the step about 'immediate safety steps'—that needs to be really clear because in some scenarios, like a suspicious package, the first thing is to evacuate and secure the area. I'll go through it carefully and flag anything that doesn't match reality.

Good points. Yes, I want to make sure the script reflects actual on-site constraints. Once you review it, we can iterate. Then we'll need to test it with at least two security staff members to confirm it's usable. That's part of the definition of done for T3.

I can arrange that. I know a couple of guards who can give honest feedback. But I want to make sure we also get legal to sign off on the script—especially the parts about what to say and what not to say. We don't want anyone accidentally admitting liability or saying something that contradicts our legal position.

Absolutely. I'll loop in legal once we have the revised version. Now, for the quick-reference checklists—T8—I'm thinking one-page, laminated, with the key steps for each scenario. Font large enough to read under pressure, maybe with icons or color coding. What do you think?

One page is good. Laminated is essential—we need it to survive on-site conditions. Color coding could help, but keep it simple. Maybe red for 'stop and evacuate,' yellow for 'alert management,' green for 'proceed with caution.' And definitely test the font size with people who aren't young—readability matters.

Good thinking. I'll incorporate that feedback. So the checklist will be scenario-specific, one page each, laminated, with color coding and large font. We'll test it with security ops before finalizing. That covers the design. Now, the big question: how do we make sure these are actually available on-site when needed? Print and laminate, or digital on phones, or both?

Both. Print for sure—you can't rely on phones in a real incident. Battery dies, network goes down, panic sets in. But also digital so people can access it on their phones if they want to review it beforehand. We should also post it in the control room and at key entry points.

That makes sense. So D4 is: printed and laminated copies at control room and entry points, plus digital version accessible on phones. I'll make sure the digital version is in a format that works offline. Now let's lock in the timeline: I need your feedback on the script by end of week, then we'll revise and test with security staff next week. Does that work?
End of week is tight but I can do it. I'll have comments back to you by Friday. Then next week for testing—I'll coordinate with the team.
Perfect. Once we have security staff feedback and legal sign-off, we'll finalize both the script and the checklists. That should close out T3 and T8. I'll update the team once we're done.

threads.thread_goal: Agree on media holding statements, Q&A, and channel strategy.

messages.text: I've drafted holding statements and Q&A templates for each of the five incident scenarios. The statements are designed to be brief, factual, and non-committal until we have more information. Each one acknowledges the incident, confirms we're taking it seriously, and directs people to official channels for updates. I've also mapped out the multi-channel strategy in A5—which channels we use for which scenarios, approval flow, and timing. See A3 for the statements and A5 for the channel strategy. I'd like feedback from 286680 and 47537 on tone and clarity.

I've reviewed the statements. They're solid—measured, professional, and they don't overcommit. One thing I'd suggest: add a line about our commitment to safety and transparency. That's what people want to hear in a crisis. Also, the Q&A section is good, but I'd add a few more likely questions, especially around 'what are you doing to prevent this in the future?' That's always asked.

I agree with those points. The tone is professional but also human—that's important. One thing I'd add: make sure the statements work across different languages if we're a global company. The diplomatic language should translate well. Also, the channel strategy in A5 looks good, but I want to confirm: who approves social media posts in real time? That's critical because social moves fast.

Good questions. I'll add the safety and transparency language, expand the Q&A, and make sure the statements are translation-ready. On the social media approval: I'm proposing a two-tier system. For holding statements, I or 286680 can post immediately. For anything beyond that, we need sign-off from legal and senior management. That's in the approval flow in A5, but I can make it clearer.

That approval flow makes sense. But I want to make sure legal is looped in early—not just for sign-off, but for drafting. Some of the language in the statements could have legal implications. Can we schedule a review with legal this week?
I'll reach out to legal today and get them on a call this week. They need to review A3 and A5 before we finalize. Once they sign off, we can lock in D5 and D6.

While legal is reviewing, I want to make sure we also test the statements with a small group of staff to see if they're clear and reassuring. Sometimes what sounds good to PR doesn't land the same way with regular employees. Can we do a quick pilot?

Good idea. I'll prepare a simple feedback form and we can test with maybe 10–15 people from different departments. That'll give us real-world input before we finalize. I'll coordinate with ops to identify a test group.

Perfect. So the plan is: legal review this week, staff pilot next week, then we finalize and lock in the holding statements and channel strategy. That should close out T4 and T7. Once we have legal sign-off, we can confirm D5 and D6.
I'll send out the legal review request today and the staff pilot form by tomorrow. We should have feedback by end of next week, which gives us time to revise before the drill.

next_steps.when: end of next week after legal and pilot feedback
end of next week after legal and pilot feedback

threads.thread_goal: Finalize internal briefing templates and training approach.

messages.text: I've drafted the internal staff briefing templates and training materials. The briefing template is designed for quick updates during and after an incident—short bullet points, clear status, next steps. The training deck covers the playbook overview, each scenario, roles and responsibilities, and a Q&A section. I've kept the language accessible for non-specialist staff and avoided jargon. See A4 for the briefing template and A6 for the training plan. I'd like feedback on tone and whether the content is clear enough for someone without a security background.

I've reviewed the materials. The briefing template is clean and easy to follow. One suggestion: add a section for 'what employees should do' so people know their role during an incident. The training deck is comprehensive, but 60 minutes might be tight if we include Q&A. Have you thought about breaking it into two shorter sessions or offering a recording for people who can't attend live?

Good points. I'll add the 'what employees should do' section to the briefing template. On the training format: I was thinking live sessions are better for engagement and Q&A, but I can also record it so people can watch on their own time. Maybe we do both—live sessions for the first rollout, then recordings available for new hires and refreshers. That way we get the engagement but also the flexibility.

I like that approach. Live sessions create accountability and allow for real-time questions. But recordings are essential for scale and for people who miss the live session. One thing: make sure the training includes a section on media interactions. Staff should know what to do if a journalist approaches them on-site. That's a common gap.

Good catch. I'll add a section on media interactions—basically, 'refer to PR' and don't speculate. I'll also include a few role-play scenarios so people can practice. Now, I want to do a pilot training session with a small group before we roll out to everyone. Can we schedule that for next week?

Absolutely. I can attend the pilot and give feedback. We should also have someone from security there to make sure the content resonates with them. And we'll need to time the full rollout so it happens before the drill—probably two weeks before so people have time to absorb it.

I'll coordinate with ops to find a pilot group and schedule the session for next week. I'll also prepare a feedback form so we can capture what works and what needs adjustment. Once we have pilot feedback, I'll revise the materials and we can lock in the training schedule.

One more thing: make sure the training materials align with the escalation script and checklists that 286680 and 47290 are finalizing. People need to see the same process in the training that they'll use in the checklist. Consistency is key.

Good point. I'll review the escalation script once it's finalized and make sure the training reflects the same steps. That way there's no confusion. So to recap: I'll revise the briefing template, add media interaction content, do a pilot training next week, and finalize the training format as live plus recordings. That covers T5 and T6.
Perfect. Once you have pilot feedback, we can lock in D7 and D8. I'll make sure the escalation script is ready for you to review by end of this week so you can align the training with it.

threads.thread_goal: Close out project with review process and distribution plan.

messages.text: We're at day 14 of the project. Let's do a readiness check. We have the escalation script and checklists nearly finalized, media statements and channel strategy in legal review, training materials in pilot phase, and we still need to lock in the post-incident review process and distribution plan. A1 is the master playbook document—I'll be consolidating all sections into that by end of this week. Where are we on T10 and T12?

I'm working on T10—the post-incident review process. I've drafted a template that captures what went well, what didn't, and what we need to change in the playbook. The template includes roles (who leads the review), timing (within 48 hours of an incident), and how findings feed back into playbook updates. I'll have it ready by tomorrow. For T12, I assume you're handling the consolidation and distribution?

Yes, I'm consolidating everything into A1 and managing the distribution. I'll need a final sign-off from legal and ops before we send it out. I'm planning to distribute by day 19 so people have two days to review before the drill. Can you have T10 ready by tomorrow so I can include it in the playbook?
I'll have it done by EOD tomorrow. I'll also prepare a summary document that explains the review process to the team so they understand why we're doing post-incident reviews and how to participate.

I'll have the training materials finalized by day 17, which gives you time to include them in A1. I'm also preparing a one-page summary of the training schedule and how people can access the recordings. That should go in the distribution package too.

Perfect. So the timeline is: all sections finalized by day 17, legal and ops review day 18, distribution day 19. That gives us a two-day buffer before the drill. I'll send out a distribution list today so we know exactly who gets the playbook and in what format.

One thing: make sure the distribution includes the on-site security team. They need to have the checklists and escalation script before the drill. And maybe a quick briefing call with them so they know what to expect.

Good point. I'll schedule a briefing call with security ops for day 20, the day before the drill. That way they have the materials and a chance to ask questions. I'll also make sure the checklists are printed and laminated by then.

I'll coordinate with ops on the briefing call and make sure we have all the materials ready. Also, I want to confirm: after the drill, we'll do a post-drill review using the process in T10, right? That's how we'll capture lessons learned and update the playbook for v1.1.

Exactly. The drill is a test of the playbook, and the post-drill review is how we improve it. I'll schedule the review for day 22, the day after the drill. We'll capture what worked, what didn't, and what needs to change. Then we'll update A1 and distribute v1.1 within a week. That's the continuous improvement cycle.

That makes sense. So we're on track: finalize by day 17, distribute day 19, briefing call day 20, drill day 21, post-drill review day 22. We should be in good shape. I'll make sure the training materials are polished and ready for distribution.
Great. I'll send out a final checklist by EOD today so everyone knows what's due when. We're on track to deliver a solid playbook before the drill. Thanks everyone for the effort so far.
